Chapter One, On the Formation of the Conditions for the Gathering of the Sangha; Chapter Two, On the Binding and Dissolving of Various Boundaries;
Chapter Three, On the Receiving and Relinquishing of the Precepts; Chapter Four, On the Receiving and Purifying of Robes and Medicines.

Chapter Five: Various Methods for the Uposatha; Chapter Six: Various Communities’ Summer Retreats; Chapter Seven: Various Methods for the Pravāraṇā; Chapter Eight: Various Methods for the Distribution of Robes; Chapter Nine: Various Methods for the Confession of Offenses; Chapter Ten: Miscellaneous Methods for Maintaining the Dharma. 1. Chapter One: The Formation of the Dharma through Assembled Conditions (Part I). In this first chapter on the formation of the Dharma through assembled conditions, both the ritual procedures (*vidhi*) and the underlying principles (*artha*) are addressed together; as it applies equally to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, the general framework has been presented first, while the detailed sub-sections have not yet been elaborated.

Furthermore, as the conditions encompass both formation and destruction, the characteristics of the teachings must be fully set forth; these are all listed below, with their meanings remaining free from confusion.
There are approximately one hundred and thirty-four *karmavācanā* (formal monastic procedures) in the Dharma of the Saṃgha.
The Buddha said:
“There are three types of *karmavācanā* that encompass all *karmas*: namely, the *jñapti-karman*, the *jñapti-dvitīya-karman*, and the *jñapti-caturtha-karman*.
There are thirty-nine procedures for the *jñapti-karman*;
among these thirty, twenty-seven are procedures for receiving confession.”
The procedure for the alms bowl; the procedure for evasive speech; the procedure for causing annoyance; the procedure for granting the tonsure;
the procedure for granting admission into the order; the procedure for assigning a teacher; the procedure for summoning one to enter the assembly; the procedure for questioning before the assembly;

the procedure for the harmony of the recitation of the precepts; the procedure for the Saṃgha’s confession; the procedure for the Saṃgha’s disclosure of offenses; the procedure for harmony at an improper time; and the procedure for the settlement of disputes through the recitation of the precepts.

The procedure for the *pravāraṇā* (invitation) in harmony; the abbreviated *pravāraṇā* method for difficult circumstances; the *pravāraṇā* method for increasing the practice of the Path; the *pravāraṇā* method for increasing matters of dispute; the second *pravāraṇā* method for increasing matters of dispute; the method for receiving the *kaṭhina* robe; the method for relinquishing the *kaṭhina* robe;
the first expanded method for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*); the second expanded method for the recitation of the precepts; the method for selecting and assembling wise persons;

the two methods for resolving matters by dispatching those who do not recite the *Vinaya*; the method for dispatching those who abandon the correct principle; and the *tṛṇaprastāraka* (covering with grass) method.

The appointment of messengers to the royal city for the council; the discussion of the Dharma and Vinaya by Kāśyapa; the questioning of Upāli regarding the Dharma and Vinaya; Upāli’s response regarding the Dharma; the questioning of Ānanda regarding the Dharma and Vinaya; Ānanda’s response regarding the Dharma; within the [Khandhaka on] the Seven Hundred, the motion for the discussion of the Dharma;
the motion for appointing bhikṣus to discuss the Dharma; the formal motion for the discussion of the Dharma and Vinaya; the motion for the Elder to question all matters; and the Elder’s response.
The distribution of *śalākā* (voting sticks) should be performed according to the prescribed rules;
the formal motion (*jñapti*) and the second motion (*jñapti-dvitīya-karman*) comprise fifty-seven rules;

the procedure for constructing a small dwelling, the procedure for constructing a large dwelling, the procedure for appointing a distributor of bedding, and the procedure for appointing one to announce grave offenses (*sthūlātyaya*).
27. The method for returning robes; the method for being separated from one's robes;

the method regarding bedding that has not been used for six years; the method for protecting the alms bowl; the appointment of a teacher for nuns; the prohibition against visiting families for alms and its subsequent lifting;

the method for maintaining a retinue; the method for nuns appointing someone to seek instruction; the method for nuns appointing those who go among the great assembly of monks for the *pravāraṇā*; and the method for dwelling with non-Buddhists.

The method for establishing the small boundary for receiving precepts and its dissolution; the method for establishing the boundary for the recitation hall and its dissolution; the method for establishing the great boundary and its dissolution; the method for establishing the boundary of the assembly site; the method for establishing the boundary for not losing one's robes and its dissolution; the method for establishing the small boundary for the recitation of precepts and its dissolution;

the method for establishing two shared boundaries, the method for establishing one shared boundary, and the method for establishing the shared rule regarding food—the latter three of these must have a dissolution;
and the method for granting the rule for those who are insane or deluded and its dissolution.

The procedure for receiving the [new] day; the procedure for appointing those who receive the *pravāraṇā*; the procedure for establishing and dissolving the small boundary (*sīmā*) for *pravāraṇā*; the procedure for distributing the property of the Saṃgha from the four directions;

the procedure for sending a messenger to receive the precepts and for dispatching an envoy; and the procedure for nuns performing the non-greeting toward the monks, along with its dissolution.

The method for appointing a bhikṣu to manage the quarters; the two methods for taking over an old dwelling and entrusting its maintenance to monastics and laypeople; the method for the imposition of the *pātra-pratigrahaṇa* (the bowl-covering); the method for appointing a messenger to inform the household where the *pātra-pratigrahaṇa* has been imposed; the method for the lifting of the *pātra-pratigrahaṇa*; and the method for the staff and the pouch.
The full text of the Vinaya is set forth as above.

There should be those appointed to distribute gruel, to distribute minor meals, to distribute *khādanīya* (solid food), to receive invitations, to spread bedding, to distribute bathing robes, and to distribute regular robes; they may take for themselves or give to others, and they shall appoint monks and novices as their attendants.
The thirty-eight procedures consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*):

the procedure for admonishing those who cause schism in the Saṃgha; the procedure for admonishing those who assist in causing schism in the Saṃgha; the procedure for admonishing those who slander [the Saṃgha] and are subject to banishment;

the procedure for admonishing those of evil character; the procedure for admonishing those with evil and false views; and the two procedures for admonishing and banishing śrāmaṇeras who hold evil and false views.
The method for admonishing a bhikṣuṇī who follows [a suspended monk];

the method for admonishing one who associates [with a suspended monk]; the method for admonishing one who encourages association with those who dwell near [the suspended]; the method for admonishing one who, out of anger, abandons the Triple Gem; the method for admonishing one who incites strife;
the method for admonishing one who associates with the sons of householders.
The rules for training in the *śikṣamāṇā* precepts, the rules for receiving full ordination (*upasampadā*), and the rules for repentance;

the rules for censure and their resolution, the rules for banishment and their resolution, the rules for dependence and their resolution, the rules for prohibiting entry into the homes of laypeople and their resolution;

the rules for suspension for failure to acknowledge an offense and their resolution, the rules for failure to confess and their resolution, and the rules for failure to relinquish [a wrong view] and their resolution.
The procedures for concealment (*paryuṣaṇā*), the procedure for returning to the original state (*mūlāpakarṣa*), the procedure for *mānāpya*, the procedure for rehabilitation (*āvarhaṇa*);
the procedure of recollection (*smṛtivinaya*), the procedure for those not insane (*amūḍhavinaya*), and the procedure regarding the locus of the offense (*tatsvabhāvaiṣīya*).
Regarding the *pratimokṣa-karman*, there are briefly thirty-three types.
The Buddha said:
"Once the ordination has been received through three utterances, it is called a well-performed *karman*."
The same applies to the *Poṣadha-vidhi* (the ritual for the recitation of the precepts).
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"Once the distribution of robes has been performed through face-to-face communication or mental reflection (*manasikāra*), it is termed a formal act (*karmavācanā*)."
"Later, the bhikṣus did not share [the portion] with him.
This section on "Sharing" (yìfēn) is divided into two parts:
first, the procedure consisting solely of the *pratideśanīya* (confession before another); second, the procedure involving the formal assembly (*jñapti-caturtha-karman*).
2. The Procedures for the Community and for Face-to-Face (Pratimokṣa) Recitation.
The texts encompass all schools, as listed below.
However, there are twenty-eight procedures for face-to-face recitation;

The method for receiving the three robes and the method for relinquishing them; the method for receiving the alms bowl and the method for relinquishing it; the method for receiving the sitting mat (niṣīdana) and the method for relinquishing it; the method for receiving the one hundred and one articles and the method for relinquishing them;

the method for relinquishing invitations, the method for relinquishing the precepts, the method for receiving the dependence of an invitation, the method for declaring the purity of robes, the method for declaring the purity of the alms bowl, the method for declaring the purity of medicine, the method for receiving the three types of medicine, the method for receiving the seven-day medicine, the method for the rainy season retreat (varṣā), the method for giving consent (chanda), the method for confessing pāyattika offenses, the method for confessing naiḥsargika-pāyattika offenses, the method for confessing sthūlātyaya offenses, and the method for confessing heavy duṣkṛta offenses.
The procedure for the sixfold *jñapti* regarding dew; the procedure for the gravity of another's offense;

the procedure for relinquishing the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* penance; the procedure for the performance of the *jñapti*; the procedure for the various acts of the *saṃghāvaśeṣa* following the *jñapti*; and the procedure for entering a settlement following the *jñapti*.
The procedure for a bhikṣuṇī to enter a bhikṣu monastery; the procedure for a bhikṣuṇī to request instruction;
the procedure for performing the *kṛta-śeṣa-bhakṣaṇa* (the ritual of leftover food); and the five procedures for the community performed in the presence of another.

The *naiḥsargika-pāyattika* dharmas, the method for reciting the precepts (*poṣadha*), the method for the invitation to criticism (*pravāraṇā*), the method for receiving offerings obtained by the Saṃgha, and the method for receiving the property of the five groups of deceased persons.
Briefly, there are fourteen types of *jñapti-karman* (formal acts performed by mental reflection);
when categorized by their meaning, they are divided into three distinct groups.
1. Mindfulness of the Dharma by oneself alone;
2. Mindfulness of the Dharma in the presence of another;
3. Mindfulness of the Dharma within a community.

These are common to all schools and will be required according to the specific texts; however, regarding the formal procedures of the Saṃgha (saṃghakarma), they are found exclusively in the *Dharmaguptaka* Vinaya.
Within this, there are three types of mental recitation (manasikāra) methods:

the method for repenting minor duṣkṛta offenses, the method of the six recollections (ṣaḍ-anusmṛti), and the method for confessing various offenses during the session of the recitation of the precepts (poṣadha).
There are seven methods for the procedure of formal declaration and mental recollection:

the method for the rainy season retreat (*varṣā*), the method for the declaration of purity (*śuddhi-ārocana*), the method for receiving medicine, the method for receiving the seven-day permit, the method for receiving and maintaining the three robes, the method for relinquishing the three robes, and the method for receiving and maintaining the alms bowl.
There are four procedures for the mental recitation (*manasikāra*) of the community of dharmas:

the procedure for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), the procedure for the invitation to criticism (*pravāraṇā*), the procedure for receiving gifts obtained by the Saṃgha, and the procedure for receiving the clothing and belongings of deceased members of the five groups.
The preceding section briefly clarifies the gathering of conditions; the subsequent section analyzes the formation and disintegration of conditions.
Regarding the former clarification of the monastic law (*saṃghadharma*), the Buddha stated in the *Vinaya*:
“There are four kinds of Saṃghas:
first, a Saṃgha of four persons; with the exception of the ordination, the *pravāraṇā*, and the rehabilitation from offenses (*āpatti-vyutthāna*), all other *karmans* should be performed by them.
Second, a Saṃgha of five persons; with the exception of the ordination in the Central Land and the rehabilitation from offenses.”
Third, there is the assembly of ten monks, excluding the rite for the removal of offenses;
fourth, there is the assembly of twenty monks, for whom all *karmavācanā* rites should be performed, let alone those exceeding twenty.
"If even one person is missing, it is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and does not succeed.
First, weighing the preceding matter;
the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states:
"Affairs refer to persons and dharmas.
The *Vinaya* states:
"One evaluates bhikṣus and laypeople; one evaluates the *karmavācanā*, the offenses, and the affairs."
However, the conditions for such actions do not exceed three types: namely, persons (*pudgala*), dharmas (*dharma*), and matters (*vastu*).
For instance, acts such as receiving the precepts, repentance, appointing officials, and disciplinary expulsion are performed for the sake of persons;
whereas acts such as the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*) and the invitation for criticism (*pravāraṇā*) are performed for the sake of dharmas.
Such matters as the demarcation of boundaries, the gathering of robes, the purification of ground, and storehouses are performed for specific purposes.

Whether conducted collectively or individually, and whether separated or combined at different times, each must first be carefully measured and evaluated to ensure that the conditions established accord with the Dharma.
2. The locus upon which the Dharma arises.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"In a place that is not a site for formal ritual action (*karmabhūmi*), one may neither receive a proxy vote (*chanda*) nor perform monastic affairs."
In the *Vinaya*, when performing a formal act (*karmavācanā*), one must first establish the boundary (*sīmābandha*).
Regarding the basis for this, there are two types:
if it is within the natural boundary (*prakṛtisīmā*), there is only the single method of the formal act for establishing the boundary.
As for the remaining monastic rules (*saṃghadharma*), they are all performed within the ritual boundary (*karmabhūmi*).
If they involve the two methods of face-to-face communication (*pratimukha*) or mental recollection (*manasikāra*), they apply to both types of boundaries.
Third, the method for assembling the Saṃgha;
The *Vinaya* states:
"The Buddha said:
'You should spread out the seats, strike the *gandī*, and all gather together in one place.'"
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"Whatever makes a sound—whether wood, tile, copper, or iron—let a *karmadāna* or a *śrāmaṇera* strike it."
"If there is no novice (śrāmaṇera), a bhikṣu may also do so;
however, it must not exceed three rounds.
In the *Dharmatrāta-dharmagupta-avadāna* (付法藏傳), the method of "long striking" (長打) is prescribed.
The *Sāhasrika-vinaya* (Three Thousand Dignified Manners) clearly explains the number of strikes for the gong.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"When assembling the Saṃgha with the gaṇḍī, there must always be a fixed standard; they may not be interchanged."
4. The Assembly Gathers and Delimits the Boundary:
Now, there are two kinds of boundaries.

If they are formal boundaries established through ritual action (*dharmakarma*), there are only three types: namely, the Great Boundary (*mahāsīmā*), the Precept Platform (*sīmāmaṇḍala*), and the Small Boundary (*khuḍḍakasīmā*).
If one discusses the small boundary (*kṣudrasīman*), there is no external area to assemble from.
If it concerns the ritual platform (*sīmāmaṇḍala*) or the great boundary (*mahāsīman*), the assembly must be summoned by proclaiming the limits in their entirety.
As for the natural boundary (*prakṛtisīman*), it is divided into four distinct types: namely, the village, the wilderness (*araṇya*), the traveling path, and the water boundary.
Regarding the initial mention of a "village" (*grāma*), there are two types:

if the boundaries of the village cannot be clearly distinguished, one should follow the measurement of seven trees from the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, which calculates to six intervals totaling sixty-three paces; if there are no other groups present, the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) may be performed.
If the village boundaries can be clearly distinguished, one should follow the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* (Daśādhyāya-vinaya) and assemble all members of the village.
Second, regarding the term *araṇya* (wilderness), there are also two types:

if it is free from difficulties, many schools state it should be "one *krośa*," which, according to the *Saṃyukta-ratnapiṭaka*, is equivalent to "five *li*"; this is traditionally accepted as the standard.

If it is a wilderness characterized by difficulties, such as the measurement of "seven *paṇḍa*" mentioned in the *Sammohavinodanī*, where one may perform *karmavācanā* (formal ritual acts) at a distance of fifty-eight paces, four feet, and eight inches.

Regarding the third, the boundary of the path of practice (*pratipad-dharmaparyāya-sīmā*): according to the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* and the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, it is six hundred paces in length and breadth.

Regarding the fourth, the boundary of water (*udaka-sīmā*): as stated in the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*, it extends as far as the range reached when a strong person among the assembly on a boat throws water or sand in all four directions.

Regarding these six characteristics, it is said that the assembly of monks must be gathered within the boundaries of the specific direction facing the body or face; only when there is no one outside [the boundary] can the rite accord with the Dharma.
Fifth, the harmony of the assembly according to the Dharma;
as the *Vinaya* states:
"Those who ought to come have come; those who ought to give their consent have given their consent; those present who are entitled to censure do not censure.
This is called 'concord.
The opposite of these three conditions constitutes a 'separate assembly.'"
6. Distinguishing between those who belong to the assembly and those who do not;
the *Vinaya* states:
"Those who have not received full ordination must depart," and so forth.
It is further said that there are four "complete numbers" (*pūrṇasaṃkhyā*):

first, there are those who have attained the complete number and should not be censured; these are the four types of persons for whom the formal acts (*karman*) of censure, expulsion, probationary dependence, or prohibition from entering the homes of laypeople have been performed.
Second, there are those who, though not completing the required number, should be censured; this refers, for example, to one who intends to receive the full ordination (*upasampadā*).

Third, there are those who neither complete the required number nor should be censured; this refers to when a *karmavācanā* is being performed for a *bhikṣu*, yet the number is completed by including a *bhikṣuṇī*, a *śikṣamāṇā*, a *śrāmaṇera*, or a *śrāmaṇerī*.

If one says that those who have committed the thirteen grave offenses such as the "borderline crimes," those who have been subjected to the three types of formal accusations, those who have been expelled or are subject to expulsion, those in a period of separate residence (*parivāsa*), those on the boundary platform (*sīmāmaṇḍala*), those who possess supernormal powers and are in the air, those who have become invisible, those who are out of sight or hearing, or the person for whom the *karmavācanā* is being performed—these twenty-eight kinds of persons are not to be counted.
Furthermore, it says:
"Those who practice *parivāsa*, *mūlāpakarṣa*, *mānatva*, and those undergoing *ābṛhaṇīya*. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"The completion of *parivāsa*, the completion of *mūlāpakarṣa*, and the completion of the six nights. Regarding these seven types of persons, the Buddha said:
"They are not counted.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* further states:

"A sleeping person, a person speaking incoherently, a person in a state of commotion, a person entered into meditative concentration, a mute person, a deaf person, a person both mute and deaf, a mad person, a person with a distracted mind, a person whose mind is impaired by illness, a bhikṣu on a tree, and a layperson."
"These twelve types of persons do not constitute a quorum for receiving the precepts.
The *Mātṛkā-śāstra* states:
"A person who is gravely ill, a person from a frontier region, and a person who is dull-witted—these three types of persons do not complete the assembly."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:

"If one has given their consent (*chandadāna*), or if there is a physical barrier, or if there is a partial covering with a barrier between, or if there is a partial covering where hands cannot reach across, or if all are sitting in the open air where hands cannot reach across."
It is further stated:
"If the Saṃgha performs a *karmavācanā* while walking, it is contrary to the Dharma; the same applies even if they perform it while standing, sitting, or lying down."
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"I went to the place where the precepts were being recited but did not sit down, thereby creating a separate assembly.
The Buddha said:
"It is contrary to the Dharma.
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The sick person [performed] the *karmavācanā* and the recitation of the precepts behind their back."
The Buddha said:
"It is a separate assembly.

This definition includes those who are intoxicated, or cases where one speaks before others but they do not understand, or where the mind and the object do not correspond; all such instances are termed *adharma* (unlawful).
Therefore, within the *Vinaya*’s section on "The Method for Receiving and Renouncing the Precepts," it says:
"If one is asleep, intoxicated, insane, or enraged, such that there is no mutual understanding—as in the aforementioned circumstances—the [act] is not accomplished."

Furthermore, one must understand the distinctions among the four permutations regarding the insufficiency of the quorum for a separate assembly (*pṛthaggaṇa*), and exercise clear discernment regarding the conditions for success or failure according to the specific situation.
Fourth, there are those who, even when the quorum is complete, are still subject to censure.
If virtuous bhikṣus dwell within the same boundary, remaining within range of sight and hearing, and even inform a bystander—those who possess both of these conditions together.
Seventh, the declaration of *chanda* (consent) and *pārisuddhi* (purification); the *Vinaya* states:
"Those bhikṣus who do not attend shall declare their *chanda* and *pārisuddhi*."
Within this, there are three types: namely, the giving of consent (*chanda*), the receiving of consent, and the declaration of consent.

If there are matters concerning the Buddha, Dharma, or Sangha, or matters concerning the sick or those tending to the sick, it is permitted to give consent, with the sole exception of the single rite of establishing a boundary (*sīmā-bandhana*).
There are five ways of conveying the consent (*chanda*):

if one says, "I give you my consent"; or if one says, "I speak my consent"; or if one says, "Speak my consent for me"; or if one manifests the physical signs; or if one explains the giving of consent in detail—these constitute the successful conveyance of consent.
If one neither displays the signs nor speaks with the mouth, it is not accomplished; one should further grant the *chanda* (consent) to another.
It is also said:
"The *chanda* and the *pārisuddhi* (purification) must be declared simultaneously; they may not be declared separately."
If one wishes to explain this in detail, one should properly maintain dignified deportment and go before the person to whom the *chanda* (consent) is to be transmitted, speaking as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind!"
"Venerable Saṃgha, I, bhikṣu [Name], grant my consent and my purity regarding the legal business of the Saṃgha.
Having said this once, he should stop.
The Buddha said:
"If you can remember their names, characteristics, and categories, you may accept as many as you wish.
If you cannot remember them, it is sufficient simply to say, 'Many bhikṣus have given their consent and purity.'"
2. Clarifying the Method for Receiving the *chanda* (consent). The Buddha said:

"If one who has received the *chanda* passes away after receiving it; or if they go beyond the boundary; or if they abandon the path; or if they join the assembly of non-Buddhists or a separate faction; or if they arrive at the site of the precept-platform (*sīmā-śālā*); or if any of the seven conditions such as the appearance of dawn occur—these, along with the aforementioned twenty-eight conditions including declaring oneself to be one who has committed a *pārājika* offense or other persons subject to the thirteen obstacles, those subject to the three formal accusations (*ukkhepanīya-kamma*), those subject to the two types of exclusion (*nissaya*), being in the air, being invisible, or being out of sight and hearing—all such cases do not constitute a valid reception of the *chanda*."
"If one reaches the middle of the path, or if one is among the Saṃgha, it is likewise; one should further give one's *chanda* (consent) to another.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states that there are five ways of losing one's *chanda*, as explained in the section on "those not counted" (*asaṃkhyeya*).

It is further stated: "Receiving the *chanda* (consent) outside the boundary; the holder of the *chanda* leaving the boundary; the person giving the *chanda* leaving the boundary; having given the *chanda*, one returns to the midst of the Saṃgha and then departs from the assembly; fifth, while holding the *chanda* within the Saṃgha, one is startled by a difficulty and rises up, and not a single person remains—cases such as these are all termed 'loss of the *chanda*.'"
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"Those who conceal [their offenses] and three other types of persons lose their consent (*chanda*).
The *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya* states:

"Among the four types of persons such as nuns, the three types of persons such as those who are insane, or when the assembly has been improperly dismissed, the formal act of desire (*chanda*) is not accomplished.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"Regarding the person who takes the formal act of desire and the person who provides purity (*pariśuddhi*), if at the time of taking it or after it has been taken, they say of themselves, 'I am not a bhikṣu,' the purity of the formal act of desire is not accomplished."
The *Vinaya* states:
If a bhikṣu holding the consent (*chanda*) has personal business arise and is unable to go to the Saṃgha, it is permitted to transfer and bestow it upon another bhikṣu. He should speak as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with one-pointed mind!..."

I, bhikṣu [name], together with many bhikṣus, have received the consent (*chanda*) and purity (*śauca*). Both they and I shall provide our consent and purity for the legal monastic affairs (*dharmika saṃghakārya*).
3. Clarifying the Procedure for Communicating the Consent (*chanda*).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"One must not arbitrarily grant one's consent to another; it should be granted only to a monk capable of conveying that consent and speaking it within the Saṃgha."

If there is someone who speaks on their behalf, after the *karmadāna* has questioned them as above, that person who has received the consent (*chanda*) and purity (*pariśuddhi*) should respond as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This bhikṣu named so-and-so—having received his consent and purity—I convey his consent and purity regarding the legal matter of the Saṃgha."
When it is time for the *pravāraṇā*, one should say:
"I give my consent (*chanda*) and perform the *pravāraṇā*. The rest of the wording is as above.
The Buddha said:
"If one who indulges in sensual desires is asleep, in meditative absorption, forgetful, or does not act intentionally, it is still established [as an offense].
If one deliberately fails to speak of it, one incurs a *duṣkṛta* (wrongdoing)."

Fearing that the illness might worsen or cause agitation, the Saṃgha may go to the patient's location or perform the rite outside the boundary; it is not permissible to perform it separately from the assembly.

the *Vinaya* states:

If one performs a communal rite of *pratimokṣa*, such as the forfeiture and confession (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*) or the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*).

Hereafter, the dharma for a single person is explained.
If it is merely a mental recitation (manasikāra) regarding the Dharma, the matter pertains to both realms, yet only a single person may perform it;

if it is a mental recitation performed in the presence of another (pratyekamukha-manasikāra) or a mental recitation performed within a formal assembly (gaṇa-dharma-manasikāra), the realm pertains to both locations, yet there must be other persons present.
These are listed as before in the "Compilation of the Dharma" (Jifa).
The three characteristics are clearly defined and must not be compromised at the time of performance; otherwise, the ritual will fail.
Having briefly explained the conditions for accomplishing the dharma above, I shall now clarify the characteristics of what is non-dharmic.
Regarding the *saṃgha-dharma-karman*, there are seven types of improper [procedures].
The Buddha said:
"There are seven *karman* that are illegal and should not be performed."
"First, there are legal procedures (*karmavācanā*) that are neither in accordance with the Dharma nor with the Vinaya:

namely, one person censuring one person, up to the Saṃgha censuring the Saṃgha; performing a single proclamation (*jñapti*) or many proclamations; performing a single formal act (*karman*), many formal acts, or a mixture of single, two-part, and four-part formal acts; or where there is illness but no medicine, or medicine but no illness, such that the matter and the Dharma applied do not correspond."
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states:
"If one performs a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) with unclear speech," such individuals,
dharmas, and matters are not included within the initial [categories].
Second is the *karmavācanā* of an illegal separate assembly:
that is, when one announces a certain matter but performs the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) for another matter, it is called "illegal.

It is called a "separate assembly" because those who ought to come do not come; those who ought to give their consent (*chanda*) do not give their consent; and those present who are entitled to censure actually censure [the proceedings].
Third, an illegal *karmavācanā* performed by a united assembly;
"illegal" is as previously defined, while "united" is the opposite of the preceding [case].
Fourth, a legal *karmavācanā* performed by a divided assembly;
To perform what is contrary to the Dharma as if it were the Dharma is the same as the previous case of a separate assembly.
Fifth, the *karmavācanā* of a separate assembly that resembles the Dharma:
this refers to performing the formal motion (*jñapti*) after the *karmavācanā*, which is called "resembling the Dharma."
The separate assembly is as before.
Sixth, the *karmavācanā* of concordant dharma;
"concordant dharma" is as described above, and "concordance" is as before.
Seventh is the *karma* of censuring one who does not cease [from misconduct].
This refers to a formal act (*karma*) performed in accordance with the Dharma, which requires the Sangha to perform it collectively.
Now, if those who would censure it do so while the act remains in accordance with the Dharma;
If one continues to transgress despite being rebuked, it is termed "unrighteous" (*adharma*).
Seven types of unrighteousness are established according to this principle:

while the *Vinaya* bases its classification on specific cases, dividing them into seven categories according to those cases, here we seek the meaning to encompass all forms of unrighteousness exhaustively.

That is to say, there are thirty-nine types of *jñapti-karman* (formal acts consisting of a single motion), each having its own non-characteristic; their meaning is the same, though the specific faults differ.
The *jñapti-dvitīya* and *jñapti-caturtha* [karman] are likewise similar in this regard.
If these were not explained individually, the seven types of non-transgression would not be clearly manifested.

For now, we shall explain the seven non-transgressions in detail with respect to the single dharma of the *jñapti* (formal announcement) for the recitation of the precepts; the remaining three types may be understood by analogy with this example.
First, the invalidity of the person (*pudgala-ayoga*):

this refers to failing to repent for known transgressions, failing to disclose doubtful offenses, performing the ritual separately within the boundary, and so forth—cases where the person is not fit for the Dharma.
Second, the invalidity of the Dharma (*dharma-ayoga*).

This refers to cases such as when three or fewer people perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) for the recitation of the precepts (*poṣadha*), or when the procedure is inverted, omitted, or interrupted; when there is censure that does not cease; or when the recitation is unclear.
Third, the matter is improper:

this refers to the time being unsuitable for the formal teaching, the extensive or abbreviated versions lacking a valid reason, the ritual requisites being incomplete, or the boundary (*sīmā*) not being established according to the noble regulations.
Fourth is the non-existence of person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-abhāva*);
this refers to the two types of non-existence, wherein only phenomena exist and persons do not.
Fifth is the non-existence of person and activity (*pudgala-karma-abhāva*).
Although the Dharma should guide human affairs, human conduct may deviate from it.
Sixth, when the Dharma and the matter are at odds;
or although a person may accord with the Dharma, when these two are discordant, it is called "ruination."
Seventh, regarding persons, dharmas, activities, and non-activities:
these three characteristics are all non-existent, as should be understood by analogy with what preceded.
In principle, one must systematically organize all conditions and clearly comprehend success and failure.

Therefore, even when the Buddha was in the world, performing a single matter in five different places simultaneously constituted a violation of the Dharma; how much more so now in this age of the Semblance Dharma—how could one act with such negligence?
One must never be indolent or disrespectful regarding the meaning of the teachings.
The *pratimukha-karman* (act performed before another) also possesses seven types of non-validity;
this is divided into two parts.
Regarding the *pratimukha* procedure alone, only the single method of "holding the robe" (*cīvara-dhāraṇa*) is taken to illustrate the characteristics of non-validity.
Other masters explain that the various types of rites for purification and so forth differ in their objects (ālambana).
First, regarding the person:

it is improper [to perform them against] one who has committed a grave offense (pārājika) or possesses the obstacles and impediments (antarāyika-dharma), or one who has been censured; alternatively, they may be performed in the presence of both the Sangha and laypeople.
2. Error regarding the Dharma:
This refers to holding the Dharma incorrectly or with omissions, and explaining it without clear understanding.
3. Error regarding the matter;
That is to say: to commit an offense involving the forfeiture of extraneous property, which is inconsistent with the holy teaching;
or to possess the five great colors or superior colors, such that the possession is invalid.
Fourth, the non-correspondence between person and dharma.
5. Wrongness regarding persons;
6. Wrongness regarding matters and dharmas;
7. Possessing all three kinds of wrongness.
As understood from the preceding examples, the characteristics of the interwoven consciousnesses are thus.

If various dharmas are addressed face-to-face, they likewise possess seven types of non-transgressions (*avadya*). Now, taking one dharma—the offense of forfeiture and transgression (*naiḥsargika-pāyattika*)—as an example, I shall provide a detailed explanation; the others are to be understood by analogy, with their respective differences.
First, invalidity regarding the persons (*pudgala-apatti*):

this refers to a separate assembly within the boundary; the persons are not in accordance with the Dharma. Even if they perform a formal act of censure, if they merely stop short of it, it is invalid. Second, invalidity regarding the Dharma (*dharma-apatti*): [the formal act itself is not in accordance with the Dharma].
To perform a confession and return the property while various dharmas deviate from the correct path constitutes three types of invalidity:
first, the matter itself is improper;

second, regarding the robes and property acquired through transgressions, as determined by the *Vinaya*, these certainly were not established by the Noble One, and logically there can be no confession or relinquishment of them.

Furthermore, one recognizes the characteristics of the offense and applies the formal act; it is not due to doubt or an excessive application of the rule, but rather constitutes the offense of ignorance for applying it in violation [of the requirements].
Fourth, there is the non-validity of both person and dharma, continuing thus up to the seventh, which possesses all three types of non-validity.
The manifest characteristics are as described above.
The *karmavācanā* performed through mental recitation also possesses seven types of invalidity (*asamyak*);
among these, there are three:

Initially, one merely contemplates the Dharma in the mind; this refers exclusively to taking up the confession of minor *duṣkṛta* offenses with full understanding, while other cases follow similar patterns of agreement or difference.
First, "person versus non-person":
this means confessing before another person, as the substance of the act is not Buddhist.
2. Non-compliance with the Dharma (dharmavipatti):
This refers to merely thinking it in one's mind without speaking it aloud; or, although spoken, it is not clear and distinct; or there is addition, subtraction, error, or forgetfulness.
3. Non-compliance with the matter (vastuvipatti): [The text continues:]...
Due to the circumstances of the matter or through error, an offense may be light or heavy;
or the object may involve many individuals, such that the preceding characteristics have not yet been fully understood.
Fourth, there is the non-conformity of person and dharma, continuing up to the seventh case, which possesses all three types of non-conformity.
Whether it be the *pratideśanīya* (confession before another) or the mental recitation (*manasikāra*) performed by a group, each possesses seven types of "non-[proper] acts" (*avadya*).

Whether the individuals involved constitute a general assembly or a specific sub-assembly, and whether the boundary (*sīmā*) or the conditions (*pratyaya*) pertain to one of two locations, all must be determined according to these precedents; one should understand them clearly in accordance with the specific circumstances.
2. Section on the Binding and Unbinding of Various Boundaries (Part One). Section Two: The Binding and Unbinding of Various Boundaries. There are three types of boundaries:
the boundary for gathering the Saṃgha, which gathers people together in one place so as to prevent the offense of having a separate assembly;
and the boundary for gathering robes, which gathers robes to belong to a person so as to prevent the offense of leaving them overnight.

Regarding the inclusion of the food boundary (*bhojana-sīma*): by including the food within the boundary, one prevents the Sangha from being obstructed and ensures that there is no offense of "storing cooked food overnight.
This is the intended meaning of the school.
First, concerning the methods for establishing and dissolving the Sangha boundary (*saṃgha-sīma*), there are three types of Sangha boundaries:
First is the great boundary (mahā-sīmā);
second is the boundary for the precept-platform (śīla-maṇḍala); third is the small boundary (kṣudra-sīmā).

Now, within the great boundary there are further three types: namely, the identity of both persons and dharma; the identity of both dharma and food; and the identity of dharma with the separation of food.
Initially, there was only the fundamental regulation; later, exceptions were made according to circumstances.
When the formal procedure for establishing the first great boundary (mahā-sīmā) was being performed, the Saṃgha of the four directions assembled until they were utterly exhausted. The Buddha said:
"I allow you to establish a boundary according to the specific location where you reside; all must assemble there, and the proxy consent (chanda) of others is not permitted."

Among these, the resident bhikṣus should proclaim the boundary marks for the four directions of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā); if there are mountains, trees, forests, ponds, cities, moats, villages, or houses, they should mention whichever are present.
It must be established according to the meaning, with the procedure as previously described.
Once the seven conditions are complete within the monastic law (*saṃghadharma*), a single bhikṣu should address the Saṃgha, saying:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
I, the long-resident bhikṣu, shall proclaim for the Saṃgha the characteristics of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) in the four directions:

from the marker at a certain place in the southeast corner, to the marker at a certain place in the southwest corner; from there to the marker at a certain place in the northwest corner; from there to the marker at a certain place in the northeast corner; and from there back to the marker at a certain place in the southeast corner.
"This completes one circuit of the external boundary marks of this great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).
There will inevitably be curves; these must be described according to their actual form, and one must specifically point out the limits, dimensions, and locations."

Because the boundaries were not properly defined, the formal act of binding was not accomplished; thus, the *karmavācanā* was established in vain, and rituals such as the reception of the precepts were all performed in empty fashion. Therefore, it is necessary to be as clear as described above.
After the formal proclamation has been made three times, the Buddha said:

"From within the assembly, one should appoint a person to perform the *karmavācanā*—whether it be the senior monk (*sthavira*), the next-ranking monk, one who recites the Vinaya, or one who does not recite the Vinaya—who is capable of performing the *karmavācanā*."
After the question and answer were concluded, he made this formal announcement:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This resident bhikṣu has proclaimed the boundaries of the great perimeter (mahā-sīmā) in the four directions."
If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent:
the Saṃgha now establishes a great boundary within these four marks, as a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
The motion is as follows:
“Venerable Sangha, listen!
This bhikṣu residing here proclaims the marks of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) of the four directions.”
The Saṃgha now establishes a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) within these four directional markers, constituting a single residence and a single recitation of the precepts.

Those elders who consent to "the Saṃgha now establishing a great boundary within these four directional markers, constituting a single residence and a single recitation of the precepts," remain silent; those who do not consent, speak.
"The Sangha has consented to 'bind a great boundary within these four directional markers, as a single residence and a single recitation of the Prātimokṣa.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
When the procedure for dissolving the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) is being performed, if the bhikṣus wish to make it wider or narrower, the Buddha said:
"If you wish to alter it, first dissolve the previous boundary; thereafter, you may make it wide or narrow according to your intention."
"It should be understood in this way:
'Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
These bhikṣus residing in this dwelling place share the same residence and recite the Prātimokṣa together.'"
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant its consent:
the boundary is hereby dissolved.
This is the formal announcement (*jñapti*).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣus residing in this dwelling place share the same residence and the same recitation of the Prātimokṣa; we now dissolve the boundary (*sīmā*).

Those elders who consent to 'the Saṃgha dissolving the boundary for those sharing the same residence and the same recitation of the Prātimokṣa' should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak."
"The Sangha has already consented to 'hear the lifting of the boundary for those dwelling in the same residence and reciting the Prātimokṣa together.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."

Regarding this single *karmavācanā*, it is understood to apply universally to both those who have a *sīmā* (monastic boundary) and those who do not, because the text contains no restrictive limitation.

As for the method of establishing a *dharmalābha-sāmānya-sīmā* (a boundary for the commonality of Dharma and material benefits), at that time there were two separate residences where the *poṣadha* was observed separately and material offerings (*lābha*) were received separately; [the monks] now desired to observe the *poṣadha* together and receive material offerings in common.
The Buddha said:
"I permit you to dissolve the boundaries individually. You should all assemble in one place; you must not receive the *chanda* (consent).
You should proclaim the characteristics of the directions and bind them together."

The concluding formula is largely the same as before, with the sole difference being: "The Saṃgha establishes a great boundary (mahā-sīmā) at both these places, for the common recitation of the Prātimokṣa and the common distribution of offerings."

Regarding the method for establishing a boundary for a common *dharma* but distinct *lābha*: at that time, there were two monastic residences where the *poṣadha* was recited separately and offerings (*lābha*) were received separately; [the monks] now wished to have a common *poṣadha* but distinct offerings.
The Buddha said:
“Each should untie and release their bonds.
The text is abbreviated and is the same as before.
Furthermore, there were two monasteries that wished to perform the *poṣadha* separately but share the same offerings (*lābha*), for the sake of protecting their respective dwellings.
The Buddha said:
"I permit this."
Regarding these articles and dharmas belonging to the Saṃgha of the four directions:

when the dharma for delimiting the boundary of the precept-field (*sīmā-bandha*) is being performed, there may arise matters requiring a formal act (*karmavācanā*) by a group of four bhikṣus, or matters arising that require a group of five, ten, or twenty bhikṣus.
The great assembly gathered there became utterly exhausted, so the Buddha said:

"I permit you to establish a *sīmā* (monastic boundary). You may designate the characteristics of the four boundaries—whether by planting stakes, using stones, or marking the limits—and thus establish the demarcations."
The *Vinayamātṛkā* states:
"It must be surrounded by a great boundary (*mahā-sīmā*).
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* and other vinayas require that [the boundary] be established prior to the great boundary.
If one wishes to establish it, first install three tiers of boundary markers:
the innermost tier is called the outer boundary of the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept platform);

Once these three markers have been established, the monks within the natural boundary (*prakṛti-sīmā*) assemble inside the designated area of the *sīma-maṇḍala*. First, one bhikṣu should be instructed to proclaim the external boundary marker of the *sīma-maṇḍala*, speaking as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
The bhikṣus of this dwelling place shall proclaim the boundary marks for the small four-sided boundary for the Saṃgha:

from this southeastern corner marker at this dwelling place, turning west to the southwestern corner marker; from here, turning north to the northwestern corner marker; from here, turning east to the northeastern corner marker; and from here, turning south back to the southeastern corner marker.
"This completes one circuit of the outer boundary of the *śīmaṇḍala*.
After saying this three times,
if there are any curves or irregularities, they should be described according to the actual situation.
The *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is as follows: after the assembly has reached consensus as described above, one should announce:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This resident bhikṣu declares the marks of the small boundary (*sīmā*) for the four directions."
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent:
the Saṃgha now intends to establish a *karmavastu* (precept platform) within the boundaries of this small four-sided boundary.
This is the motion (*jñapti*).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!

This resident bhikṣu has proclaimed the boundaries of the small four-sided area. The Saṃgha now establishes a *kṣetra* (boundary for disciplinary acts) within these proclaimed boundaries of the small four-sided area."
"Whichever elders consent to 'the Saṃgha binding a boundary for the *sīmā* within these four marks,' let them remain silent; whoever does not consent, let them speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to 'binding the boundary for the *sīmā* within these four marks.'"
"Because the Saṃgha has consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Having completed the formal act, it shall be posted in a conspicuous place so that those who come later may know the boundaries of the various zones.
The remaining articles are to be understood accordingly.

Regarding the method for dissolving the *kṣetra* (boundary), there is no explicit text in the *Vinaya*; however, by analogy with the various methods for dissolving boundaries (*sīmā*), one simply reverses the "binding" (*bandhana*).
I shall now provide this by way of precedent; as the principle is sound and the phrasing is appropriate, one should speak as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The Saṃgha now assembles here at this residence to dissolve the *sīmā* (boundary).

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."
The Saṃgha now assembles here at this residence to dissolve the *sīmā* (boundary).
Those elders who consent to "the Saṃgha dissolving the *sīmā* at this assembly in this residence" should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
"The Sangha has consented to the resolution of the *karmavācanā* for the dissolution of the *sīmā-śīla-maṇḍala*.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Regarding the method for establishing a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*) containing a *śīla-maṇḍala*, the Buddha said:
"One must not form a boundary by joining river waters, except in cases where there is a permanent boat service or a bridge.
Furthermore, two boundaries must not touch one another; an interval must be left between them."
The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states:
"If the boundaries are not proclaimed, the establishment of the boundary is not accomplished.
Since the scriptural text is somewhat abbreviated, one should proclaim the boundaries as follows:

"Venerable Saṃgha, listen! I, the bhikṣu, shall proclaim the internal and external boundary marks for the four directions of the great boundary (mahā-sīmā) for the Saṃgha. First, I proclaim the internal marks:

starting from the outer corner of the southeast of the boundary of the *śīmaṇḍala* (precept platform), at a distance of about two feet beyond the marker [named so-and-so]—this refers to whatever markers were present at that time, and it is not necessary to recite the specific names—the southeast corner of this great boundary is marked by the marker named so-and-so; from here, turning westward, one reaches the southwest corner marker named so-and-so; from here, turning northward, one reaches the northwest corner marker named so-and-so; from here, turning eastward, one reaches the northeast corner marker named so-and-so."
From here, turn south and return to the marker at the southeast corner. Next, announce the outer boundary:

from this marker at the southeast corner of the dwelling site, turn west to the marker at the southwest corner; from here, turn north to the marker at the northwest corner; from here, turn east to the marker at the northeast corner; and from here, turn south, returning once more to the marker at the southeast corner.
"That is the internal marker; this is the external marker.
This completes one circuit of the internal and external markers of the great boundary.
Having chanted this three times.

If one wishes to designate the boundary marks, one should take four or five bhikṣus outside the *sīmā* (precept field) and assemble the Saṃgha within the entire area marked by the signs. After the two layers of boundary marks have been proclaimed, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is to be performed by the Saṃgha; its text is no different from the procedure for first establishing a great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), and therefore it is not set forth here.
The Method for Establishing the Three Small Boundaries (*kṣudrasīmā*). These three small boundaries were established because of various difficulties.
The *Vinaya* states:

"If there are those who do not consent, provided they have not yet left the boundary, it is permitted to assemble them quickly in one place outside the boundary and establish a small boundary to confer the precepts."
He further said:

"If, on the day of the Poṣadha, one is traveling through a wilderness where there is no village and the community of monks cannot assemble together, they should follow along with their respective teachers and virtuous friends off the main road, gather at a single location, and establish a minor boundary (kṣudrasīmā) to recite the precepts."
He further said:

"If, on the day of the *pravāraṇā*, one is traveling on a road in a non-village area or an *araṇya* and is unable to assemble [with the community], one may move to another location with one's teacher or close friends, establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*), and perform the *pravāraṇā*."
Thus we know that it is not difficult to establish a boundary without a formal motion (*jñapti*), as this is analogous to the various cases where a boundary is opened;

however, if one violates the regulations, it constitutes an offense. Furthermore, there are no external signs; rather, the very place where the body is seated serves as the substance of the boundary (*sīmā*). Therefore, in the *Upasampadā-vastu* (Section on Ordination), it says: "The Saṃgha has gathered in one place to establish a small boundary (*kṣudrasīmā*). In the *Poṣadha-vastu* (Section on the Uposatha), it says: "Now, so many bhikṣus have gathered to establish a small boundary. In the *Pravāraṇā-vastu* (Section on the Invitation), it says: "The seating places of the bhikṣus are already full; taking the seating places of these bhikṣus as the limit, the Saṃgha shall establish a small boundary therein," and so forth.

Thus we know that both [the person being censured and the one censuring] lack external characteristics; this is to refute those who would object, as stated in the *Kṣudrakavastu* on the "Method for Receiving Ordination Outside the Boundary": "If one censures from outside the boundary, the censure is not valid."
This text clearly establishes that there are no external boundary markers; it is evident.
Now, if one establishes boundary markers for a courtyard within [a larger area] and performs the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*) therein, the ritual is not valid.
This is because the boundary markers for the Great Boundary (*mahā-sīmā*) were not proclaimed according to the Dharma.
The small boundary has no defined marks;
if one were to establish it through an illegal procedure, then the large boundary would require an individual to proclaim its marks, which are subsequently recorded in the *karmavācanā* text.
