Have you not caused a schism in the Saṃgha?”
“Did you not, with an evil mind, shed the blood of a Buddha?
Are you not a non-human being? Are you not an animal?”
"Are you not of both sexes?
If he answers accordingly, "No," [the preceptor asks]: "What is your name?
What is the name of your preceptor?"
"Are you twenty years of age?
Are your three robes and alms bowl complete?
Have your parents given their permission?"
"Do you not owe debts to others?
Are you not a slave?
Are you not a government official?"
"Are you a man? A man may have such diseases as leprosy, abscesses, white leprosy, consumption, or insanity; do you now have any such disease?"
He answered each question in full according to whether the answer was affirmative or negative; as they understood the meaning of the words, he gave the same instruction as before.
Second, the Method for Formally Bestowing the Precept-Substance (*śīla-skandha*): The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:

"Whenever one wishes to receive the precepts, one must first be guided by a discourse on the Dharma to open their understanding, causing them to give rise to a mind of compassion toward all objects, whereby they shall obtain the *adhiśīla* (higher morality)."
One should say to them:

"Sentient beings in the six realms of existence mostly possess obstacles to the precepts; only humans may receive them, yet even they still harbor prohibitions and difficulties, so that not all are necessarily capable."
Since you are free from obstacles and impediments, you shall certainly receive the precepts.
You should rely on the text and give rise to the superior resolve, which is to rescue and protect all sentient beings and deliver them through the Dharma.
Furthermore, morality is the root of all virtues and can serve as the direct cause for the Three Vehicles.
Moreover, morality is a treasure within the Buddha-dharma that does not exist in other paths.
It can also protect and uphold the Buddha-dharma, causing the True Dharma to abide for a long time.
Furthermore, by the majestic power of the *karmavācanā* and the great strength of the Saṃgha, we are able to take up this supreme Dharma of the Dharma-realm and place it within your body and mind.
You should receive it with single-minded attention and careful heed.
One should make the formal announcement (*jñapti*) as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor, so-and-so."
This person, [Name], now requests from the Sangha the conferral of full ordination, with [Name] acting as preceptor.
[Name] has personally declared himself pure, free from all obstacles, twenty years of age, and fully equipped with the three robes and alms bowl.
If the time is ripe for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent and listen:
the Saṃgha shall confer full ordination upon [Name], with [Name] as the preceptor.
This is the formal motion (*jñapti*).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"After the formal motion (*jñapti*) has been made, one asks the Saṃgha: 'Is it accomplished?
This is done likewise for the first, second, and third proclamations of the formal act (*karmavācanā*)."
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:

"When receiving the precepts through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), one should listen with a single-minded focus; do not have other perceptions or other thoughts. One should treat it with reverence, maintain correct reflection, and keep it in mind with every thought. One should discern it clearly; whoever violates this incurs a *duṣkṛta* offense."
“Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
This person, [Name], seeks to receive full ordination from the preceptor [Name].
This person, [Name], now requests the Saṃgha to grant him full ordination, with [Name] as his preceptor.”
So-and-so has declared himself pure, free from obstacles, twenty years of age, and fully possessed of the three robes and alms bowl.
The Saṃgha now confers the full ordination upon So-and-so, with So-and-so as his preceptor.
"Venerable sirs, those who consent to 'the Saṃgha granting full ordination to so-and-so, with so-and-so as preceptor,' remain silent; whoever does not consent, please speak."
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
The second and third [recitations] are also as above.
Through this sequential questioning and answering, it is obtained provided there is no opposition.
“The Sangha has already consented that so-and-so be granted full ordination, with so-and-so as preceptor.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.”

The *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā* and the *Mūla-vinaya* both state: "Once full ordination has been conferred, the preceptor (*upādhyāya*), the instructor (*ācārya*), and others shall record the season—whether spring, summer, or winter—and the specific date, such as the month and day, down to the measurement of shadows, at which time the full precepts were received."

Next, regarding the time for explaining the secondary characteristics (anulakṣaṇa): there was a bhikṣu who, having received full ordination, was abandoned by the Saṃgha. Not knowing what constituted an offense, he committed a grave transgression.
The Buddha said:
"From this day forward, after the *karmavācanā* has been performed, you must first explain the four *pārājika* dharmas to him."
“Listen, son of good family!
The Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has proclaimed the four pārājika dharmas. If a bhikṣu commits even one of these dharmas, he is no longer a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya.”
"You must all refrain from committing sexual misconduct or engaging in impure practices.
If a bhikṣu commits an impure act and indulges in the dharma of sexual desire—even with an animal—he is no longer a śramaṇa, nor a son of the Śākya."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke a parable for them:

"It is just as if someone were to have their head cut off; they could never live again. So it is with a bhikṣu: once he has committed a pārājika offense, he can no longer restore his status as a bhikṣu."
"You must not do this for as long as you live. Can you maintain this?
He replied, "I can maintain it."
“Under no circumstances shall one steal, even down to a blade of grass or a leaf.

If a bhikṣu steals five coins or more from another person—whether taking it himself or instructing another to take it; whether breaking it himself or instructing another to break it; whether cutting it himself or instructing another to cut it; or whether burning it, burying it, or altering its color—he is no longer a śramaṇa, no longer a son of the Śākya.”
Just as when the heart of a tāla tree is cut off, it never again grows or flourishes;
so too it is with a bhikṣu: once he has committed a pārājika offense, he can never again restore his status as a bhikṣu.
"You must not do this for as long as you live; can you maintain this?
He replied, "I can maintain it."
“Under no circumstances shall one intentionally take the life of a living being, even down to an ant.

If a bhikṣu intentionally takes a human life with his own hand, or provides a person with a weapon, or instructs them to die, or praises death, or gives another a non-medicinal substance, or causes an abortion, or performs incantations to kill, or personally employs such means, or instructs others to do so—he is no śramaṇa, no son of the Śākya.”
The Dārṣṭāntikas say:
"Just as a needle with a broken eye is no longer fit for use, so it is with a bhikṣu; once he has committed a pārājika offense, he can no longer restore his status as a bhikṣu."
"In this regard, for as long as life lasts, you must not do so;
can you maintain this? He replied, "I can maintain it!"
“None shall speak falsely, even in jest. If a bhikṣu, when it is not true and not his own attainment, says of himself:

‘I have attained the state of a superior man—I have attained dhyāna, I have attained liberation, I have attained samādhi, I have attained the four formless attainments; I have attained the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat; gods, nāgas, and spirits come to make offerings to me.’”
"He is not a śramaṇa; he is not a son of the Śākya.
As the parable-tellers say:
'Just as a great stone split into two parts can never be joined together again, so it is with a bhikṣu; once he has committed this pārājika offense, he can no longer restore his status as a bhikṣu.'"
"You must not do this for as long as you live. Can you maintain this?
He replied, "I can maintain it."

When the Four Reliances were being conferred, there was famine in the world and it was difficult to obtain food through alms-seeking. Some non-Buddhists would suddenly leave the household life and receive the precepts, but later, when the Sangha had no food, they would immediately abandon the path.
The Buddha said, "First grant the four reliances, and only then bestow the precepts.
Later, there was a non-Buddhist who sought ordination from the Sangha; when the four reliances were first explained to him, he replied:
"I am capable of relying on two things:
rag-robes and fermented medicines; I am not capable of these other two," he said, and thereupon he abandoned the path.
The Buddha said:
"These non-Buddhists have lost much. From this day forward, the four reliances shall be conferred.
They should be conferred with these words:
“Listen, son of good family!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught the four reliances; by relying upon these, a bhikṣu attains renunciation, receives full ordination, and fulfills the dharma of a bhikṣu.”
A bhikṣu relies on rag-robes; by relying on these, he goes forth, receives full ordination, and becomes a bhikṣu according to the Dharma.
Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts?
He replied, "I can uphold it. [The Buddha said:
"If you obtain additional benefits—such as robes offered by donors or robes made from cut-up or discarded cloth—you may accept them."
"A bhikṣu relies on alms-gathering; it is by relying on this that a bhikṣu is able to go forth, receive full ordination, and achieve the status of a bhikṣu.
Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts?"
He replied, “I can uphold it! [The Buddha said:

“If you obtain long-term benefits—whether it be food assigned by the Saṃgha, food sent by a donor, food on the eighth day of the month, food on the fifteenth day, food on the first day of the month, the regular food of the Saṃgha, or food offered by invitation from a donor—you may accept it.”
“Sitting under a tree: by relying on this, a bhikṣu attains the going forth, receives full ordination, and fulfills the dharma of a bhikṣu.
Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts?”
He replied, “I can uphold it! [The Buddha said:
“If you obtain additional benefits—such as a separate room, a pointed-roofed house, a small room, a stone chamber, or two rooms with a single door—you may accept them.”
“Relying on fermented medicinal drugs, a bhikṣu relies upon these to go forth, receive full ordination, and become a bhikṣu.
Can you maintain this for as long as life lasts?”
He replied, “I can uphold it! [The Buddha said:
“If you obtain long-term benefits—ghee, oil, fresh butter, honey, or rock sugar—you may accept them.”

“Since you have already received the precepts, and the formal procedure of the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* has been accomplished according to the Dharma, and you have obtained your place, with a *upādhyāya* who is according to the Dharma and an *ācārya* who is according to the Dharma, and the community of monks being complete and sufficient—you should properly receive the instructions of the teaching; you ought to exhort and transform others, cultivate merit, repair stupas, and make offerings to the community of monks.”

If the Upādhyāya or Ācārya gives any instruction in accordance with the Dharma, you must not disobey it; you should study, recite the sūtras, and diligently seek skillful means so that, within the Buddha-dharma, you may attain the fruit of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, or Arhat.
Since you have first resolved to leave the household life, your merit shall not be in vain and its karmic fruition shall never cease.
As for other matters you do not yet know, you should inquire of your Upādhyāya and Ācārya.
The Buddha said:
"One who has received full ordination should be made to go ahead.
A disciple should inquire after his preceptor three times each day.
In the morning, at midday, and in the evening, one should perform two services for the Upādhyāya; one must not decline these even if they are laborious:
first, the repair of dwellings; second, the mending and washing of robes.
"All instructions of the Upādhyāya that are in accordance with the Dharma must be fully practiced; those who violate them shall be dealt with according to the law.

Regarding the procedure for requesting an Ācārya: at one time there was a bhikṣu whose Upādhyāya had passed away, and he intended to leave the monastic life or resolve to go beyond the boundaries of the monastery.
Because they lacked instruction, they broke various precepts and behaved in ways contrary to proper decorum.
The Buddha said:
"I permit that there be an ācārya; you should together honor, respect, and attend to him according to the rules for an upādhyāya."
One should properly maintain one's deportment and request as follows:
"Venerable sir, please attend to me with a single mind!
I, [name], now seek the Venerable sir to be my preceptor for dependence; may the Venerable sir grant me dependence, so that I may dwell in dependence upon the Venerable sir."
After this has been said three times, the preceptor must also request the authorization to maintain disciples; it is no different from the procedure for a *upādhyāya*.
Once he has accepted the request, he should reply as follows:
"It is so! I grant you my dependence; do not be negligent!
The disciple must perform two duties for him and may not decline or make excuses.

If one requests the scriptures and inquires into their meaning, and through such inquiry attains some understanding, then upon reaching a full five years [of training], one may be released from dependence.
If, however, one possesses no such knowledge and is not proficient in reciting the precepts, one must remain in dependence for as long as life lasts.

An ācārya must possess five virtues—he must know what constitutes an offense, know what does not constitute an offense, know what is light, and know what is heavy—and must have reached ten years [of standing] before he may guide others.
If one lacks these virtues, one does not rely on [a preceptor] who is faultless;
the virtues of an upādhyāya are of this same nature.
Regarding the method for the bhikṣuṇī saṃgha to confer the precepts, the *Samantapāsādikā* states:
"Ni" means "woman"; "mo" means "mother.
Because she was a Ni who was also a mother, she was so addressed.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Because nuns have attained immeasurable discipline (*saṃvara*), they should rank after the bhikṣus.
However, because of practical inconveniences regarding ritual protocol, the Buddha placed them after the śrāmaṇeras."
The *Āryābhikṣuṇī-sūtra* states:
"Women are merely deluded by physical form; they take on disciples and attend only to momentary affairs. Therefore, it is ordained that they rely upon the Great Saṃgha.

Regarding the ritual for bestowing the śrāmaṇerī precepts, the *karmavācanā* for taking on disciples, the method for shaving the hair, and the method for going forth, these are all identical to those in the [rules for] monks (*bhikṣu*), with the sole difference being the addition of the word "nun" (*bhikṣuṇī*).
The *Vinaya-mūla* on the Method for Ordaining a Śikṣamāṇā:

"Various nuns have arbitrarily granted others the going forth and the reception of precepts; because they did not know the characteristics of the precepts, they committed what is contrary to the Dharma."
The Buddha said:
"One should perform the *karmavācanā* for training in the precepts.
In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, regarding the offense of ordaining a pregnant woman without due care, the Buddha said:
"By granting the two-year *karmavācanā*, one may know whether [the precepts] exist or not.
However, the six rules purify the mind, while the two years purify the body.
Regarding the request for the method of training in the precepts, the Buddha said:

"If one who has been married for ten years, or an eighteen-year-old maiden who wishes to train in the precepts for two years, [should wish to do so], she must go before the Saṃgha, bare her right shoulder, remove her leather sandals, prostrate at the feet of the Bhikṣuṇī-saṃgha, place both knees on the ground, and join her palms. She is instructed to make this request, saying:
'Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!'"
I, the śrāmaṇerikā [Name], now request from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts, with the bhikṣuṇī [Name] as my upādhyāyikā.
May the Saṃgha grant me the two-year training in the precepts out of compassion.
After she has made the three requests,
the śrāmaṇerī should go to a place where she can see but cannot hear [the assembly] and stand there.
Within that community of nuns, the one performing the *karmavācanā* for the rules of training (*śikṣamāṇā-dharma*) should say:
"Venerable Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!
This śrāmaṇerikā so-and-so now requests from the Saṃgha the two-year training in the precepts, with nun so-and-so as her preceptor (upādhyāyī).
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent: [I shall grant it]."
"I am requesting that [Name] śrāmaṇerī undergo the two-year training in the precepts, with [Name] bhikṣuṇī as her preceptor (upādhyāyī).
This is my formal announcement.
Sisters of the Saṃgha, listen!..."
This śrāmaṇerikā so-and-so requests from the Saṃgha two years of training in the precepts, with nun so-and-so as her preceptor (upādhyāyī).
The Saṃgha now grants this śrāmaṇerikā so-and-so two years of training in the precepts, with nun so-and-so as her preceptor.

"Whichever sisters among you approve that the Saṃgha grant this śrāmaṇerī [name] the two-year training in the precepts, with the nun [name] as her preceptor, remain silent; whoever does not approve, speak."
"This is the first *karmavācanā*.
Thus it is said three times.
"The Saṃgha has already consented to grant the two-year training in the precepts to the śrāmaṇerikā so-and-so, with nun so-and-so as her preceptor; this is concluded."
"Because the Saṃgha has remained silent, this matter is thus upheld.
Next, regarding the method for reciting the characteristics of the precepts, the Buddha said:
"One should summon [the person] to enter the assembly and explain the names of the six dharmas to them."
“Listen attentively, [Name]!
The Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha has taught six rules:
‘One must not commit impure conduct; one must not engage in the practice of sexual desire.’”
If a śikṣamāṇā engages in sexual intercourse, she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā and is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.
If she touches the body of a man with a defiled mind, her precepts are deficient; she must receive the precepts again.
"Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit any transgression;
can you maintain this? He replied, "I can maintain it!"
"One must not steal, even so much as a blade of grass or a leaf.

If a śikṣamāṇā takes five coins or more than five coins from another—whether she takes it herself or instructs another to take it, whether she cuts it herself or instructs another to cut it, or burns it, buries it, or alters its color—she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā; she is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan."
"If one takes less than five coins, the precept is deficient and one must receive the precepts again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit an offense;
can you uphold it? He replied:
“Can you maintain it? “I can.
“One must not intentionally take the life of any living being, even so small as an ant.

If a śikṣamāṇā intentionally takes a human life with her own hand, or seeks out a knife and gives it to another, or instructs someone to die, or praises death, or administers non-medicinal substances, or causes an abortion, or performs incantations and sorcery—whether acting herself or instructing others to do so—she is no longer a śikṣamāṇā; she is no longer a daughter of the Śākya clan.”
If you sever the life-force of an animal that is incapable of transformation, this constitutes a deficiency in the precepts; you should receive the precepts again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit such an offense. Can you uphold this?
He replied, "I can uphold them! [The Buddha said:
"You must not speak falsely, even in jest."

If a śikṣamāṇā, being untrue and not possessing [such qualities] herself, falsely claims to have attained the state of a superior person—claiming to have attained dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, or right reception; or claiming to have attained the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, or arhat; or claiming that devas, nāgas, or yakṣas come to make offerings to her—she is not a śikṣamāṇā, nor is she a daughter of the Śākya clan.
If one intentionally utters a falsehood within the assembly, the precepts are impaired and one must receive them again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit an offense; can you uphold this?
He replied, "I can uphold it! [The Buddha said:
"One must not eat at improper times."
If a śikṣamāṇā eats at an improper time, her precepts are deficient and she must receive them again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit this offense; can you maintain it?
He replied, "I can uphold them! [The Buddha said:
"You must not drink alcohol."
"If a śikṣamāṇā drinks alcohol, she violates the precepts and must receive them again.
Within this, for as long as life lasts, you must not commit this offense; can you uphold it?
She replied:
“I can uphold them!
The Buddha said:
“A śikṣamāṇā should train in all the precepts of a full bhikṣuṇī, with the exception of taking food with her own hand and giving food to others.”
This female trainee in the Dharma must fully observe three sets of precepts:
first, the training in the root rules, which are the four grave offenses;

second, the training in the six rules, namely: intentional physical contact, stealing, taking what is not given when it is worth less than five māsakas, taking the life of an animal, speaking a minor falsehood, eating at improper times, and drinking intoxicants.
Third, the training rules (śikṣāpada): this refers to the various precepts and deportment of the great nuns, all of which are prescribed for study.
If one violates a fundamental rule (mūlāpatti), she should be expelled (pravāsanīya).
If one is deficient in the rules of training (*śikṣāpada*), they shall be granted a further two-year formal act (*karmavācanā*).

If one violates the rules of conduct, this constitutes a direct transgression of the Buddha’s teaching and must be immediately confessed; it does not, however, destroy the six fundamental rules of training already undertaken.
Regarding the method for conferring the Bhikṣuṇī precepts, the Buddha said:
"There are Bhikṣuṇīs by the Eight Respectful Precepts, Bhikṣuṇīs by 'Welcome,' and Bhikṣuṇīs who have destroyed the fetters (*saṃyojana*).

Among those receiving [the precepts] through formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), there are Bhikṣuṇīs sent by messenger, Bhikṣuṇīs who were previously married and are ten years of age, and maiden Bhikṣuṇīs of eighteen who have studied the training rules for two years and receive them from a community of twenty; in border regions, they are established by a community of ten."
"The first three [precepts] apply exclusively to the Buddha's era, while the latter five apply throughout the Semblance and Final Dharma periods.
Regarding the method for requesting permission to ordain others, the Buddha said:

"A bhikṣuṇī who has completed twelve years and wishes to ordain others should fully maintain dignified deportment, prostrate at the feet of the bhikṣuṇīs, and perform the three requests according to the rules for the bhikṣusaṃgha."
Since the phrasing is identical, it is not repeated here.
Regarding the ordination of śrāmaṇerikās, śikṣamāṇās, and bhikṣuṇīs, one must separately request permission for each.
This is because a preceptor commits an offense by ordaining disciples year after year, or because they have abandoned the rules concerning the maintenance of a following.
Regarding the method for admitting a following, the Buddha said:

"The bhikṣuṇīs should observe whether this person is capable of instructing [a candidate] in the two years of training in the precepts and can provide the two forms of support; they should then grant her the formal ritual (karmavācanā)."
The text is as above.
If one is unable to provide instruction or guidance, the *karmavācanā* (formal ritual act) is invalid.
Prior to the formal conferral of the precepts, eight conditions must be fulfilled:
1. Clarifying the Method for Requesting a Preceptor (*upādhyāya*).
The Buddha said:

"If one has been married for ten years, has studied the precepts for two years, and is twelve years of age; or if she is an eighteen-year-old maiden who has studied the precepts for two years and is twenty years of age, one should confer the full ordination upon her."
Having fully observed the proper deportment, she instructs her, saying:
"Sister, attend closely!
I, [Name], seek you, Venerable Lady, to be my preceptor; may you, Venerable Lady, act as my preceptor."
“It is because of you, Noble Lady, that I have been able to receive the full ordination; it is out of your compassion.
Having made this request three times, she replied:
"Very well. This applies likewise up to the request for two *ācāryas* and seven witnesses to the precepts.
Second, the Buddha said:
"Once the candidate for ordination has been settled so that they are out of earshot but within sight, the teacher shall be appointed.
Third, the procedure for appointing the preceptor:
therein, the preceptor should ask as follows:
"Who can act as the preceptor for [Name]?
Someone replied, "I, [Name], am able."
One should perform the formal announcement (*jñapti*) and assign [the preceptor] as follows:
"Sisters of the Sangha, listen!
This person, so-and-so, seeks to receive the full ordination from the preceptress, so-and-so."
If the time is right for the Sangha, may the Sangha listen with patience:
So-and-so shall serve as the instructor.
This is the formal motion.
4. The preceptor emerges from the assembly to inquire about the Dharma.
He should rise, prostrate at the feet of the bhikṣuṇīs, and go to where the candidate for ordination is, saying:
"Sister!..."
"This is the antaravāsaka; this is the uttarāsaṅga; this is the saṃghāṭī; this is the saṃkakṣikā; this is the kakṣapuṭa; this is the pātra."
"Are these robes and bowl yours?
He replied, "They are."
“Sister, listen!
Now is the time for truth, the time for speaking the reality.
I now question you: you should speak what is real as real, and what is not real as not real.”
"Have you not committed a bordering offense (*antāpatti*)?

This refers to one who, having previously received the five precepts, the eight precepts, or the ten precepts and committed one of the four grave offenses, or having received the full ordination (*upasampadā*) and committed one of the eight grave offenses, has returned to lay life and now comes again; such a person is called one who has committed a bordering offense.
One should answer:
"I have not committed an offense.
The following challenges and refutations are all to be conducted according to the preceding questions; for where neither party understands, it does not constitute a formal question and answer.
“Have you not violated a bhikṣu of pure conduct?
Have you not received the precepts with a thieving mind?
Have you not broken [the precepts of] either the inner or outer paths?”
"Are you not a eunuch?
Have you not killed your father?
Have you not killed your mother?"
"Have you not killed an Arhat?
Have you not caused a schism in the Saṃgha?
Have you not, with malicious intent, drawn blood from the body of a Buddha?"
"Are you not a non-human? Are you not an animal?
Are you not of both genders?"
He replied to both of them, saying,

If one says:
"I am not in accordance with the Dharma; my preceptor does not know," or if one says:
"I have transgressed the precepts, yet my upādhyāya has abandoned me and failed to instruct or admonish me.
If the disciple commits an offense and the upādhyāya abandons him, it is permissible [to speak thus].
Now, although the situation calls for censure, he fails to reprimand or question [the disciple] due to his own delusion.
"If there is an offense, one does not even know it.
Or if one says:
"Even if one has committed an offense and repented, one still does not know it."
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"One should admonish the teacher with gentle words.
If he does not accept [the advice], the upādhyāya should abandon him and go far away."

Regarding the preceptor (*upādhyāya*): "If one takes one's robes and bowl to stay overnight outside the boundary, intending to return the following day, one may rely upon another bhikṣu as a new preceptor.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"There are four kinds of preceptors:"
If both the Dharma and food are given, it is called dwelling in happiness;
if the Dharma is given but food is not, one must seek food elsewhere, which is called dwelling in suffering;
if food is given but the Dharma is not, one should offer an apology and depart.
"If one does not provide the food of the Dharma, regardless of whether it is day or night, one should immediately depart.

This is because the original intent of leaving the household life is to set one's will upon the path of practice; to be surrounded by worldly attachments is, on the contrary, to bind oneself further to birth and death. Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states:
"Because of being stained by attachment to kinsmen and delighting in dwelling places, one falls into rebirth among the hungry ghosts of the Kalinga and other realms."
The remainder is as detailed in the *Śāstra*.
Regarding the time when one is admonished for committing an offense against the Dharma: there was a bhikṣu who wished to commit a *pārājika* offense, up to and including a *duṣṭhulā* (grave) offense.
The Buddha said:
“The monks should admonish him in accordance with the Dharma,
speaking as follows:
‘Venerable one!…’”
"Do not do this; you should not act thus.
What the Venerable One has done is contrary to the Dharma, contrary to the Vinaya, and contrary to the Buddha's teaching.

If that bhikṣu says, "I have only now come to know this rule, this Sūtra of the Precepts, which comes from within the Sūtra of the Precepts recited every half-month," the other bhikṣus should again admonish him as follows:
"Elder! You have already sat through two or three recitations of the *Poṣadha* ceremony, let alone more.
Now you have gained no benefit; you have not attained what is good."
"Why is this? When you recited the precepts, you did not apply your mind, nor did you listen to the Dharma with single-minded attention.
Thus, this bhikṣu, knowing that what he had done was right and that the admonitions of others were wrong, committed a fundamental offense by acting accordingly.
If one does not comply with the instruction, it is a *duṣkṛta*.
If one knows that what one has done is wrong, yet persists in doing so because one considers the other’s admonition to be right, one commits the root offense;
if one does not comply with the instruction, it is a *pāyattika*.

If a bhikṣu is ignorant and lacks understanding, he shall be dealt with according to the Dharma for the offense he has committed; furthermore, he incurs an additional *pārajika* offense for his ignorance.
If one offers admonition to such an ignorant person, he should reply:
"You should question your teachers—the Upādhyāya and Ācārya—and further study, inquire, and recite the sūtras."
"Once you have understood the method of admonishing, you may then reprimand and advise.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya* states:
"Regarding those who are to be admonished, there are six types of persons:"

1. Having attachment and aversion in the mind; 2. having dull faculties and a lack of wisdom; 3. having little learning or insight; 4. for the sake of gain and fame; 5. for the sake of happiness in the present life, desiring only to discipline oneself; 6. if one has newly gone forth from the household life, being attached to wife and children.
Regarding these six types of persons, admonishing them will only cause harm; if one offers instruction and admonition, their words will be of no benefit. One should instead respond with these words:
"Observe only your own conduct as wholesome or unwholesome; do not observe whether others act or refrain from acting."
"If one reverses these six points, then they should exhort and admonish one another.
When there was a bhikṣu who did not study the precepts nor praise the precepts as he committed violations, the Buddha said:
"The other bhikṣus should admonish him in accordance with the Dharma."
He spoke thus: "Venerable sir! One should train in the precepts and praise the precepts;

one should not destroy them oneself, one should not commit offenses, and one should not be rebuked by the wise. Thus one will receive immeasurable merit and enjoy peace and happiness for a long night."
If that bhikṣu should say:
"Venerable sir!
What is the use of these minor rules of training?"
"I will not study this precept now; I shall instead question other wise bhikṣus who uphold the Vinaya.
The other bhikṣus should again admonish him, saying:
"Venerable sir, do you speak these words because you wish to cause the destruction of the Dharma?"

Since you, Venerable One, do not study the precepts, do not praise the precepts, and have yourself violated them, committing many offenses, you are censured by the wise and shall suffer for a long night, finding no peace or happiness.
If that monk being admonished is deluded and does not understand, the monk who is admonishing him should reply to him, saying:
"Go back and ask your preceptor.
The rest of the text is as above; having admonished him in accordance with the Dharma, he should continue the admonition.
If one wishes to know and study [the Vinaya], one should pose difficult questions.
The Buddha said:
"There are five ways of upholding the Vinaya:..."
If one recites from the *Śīlaskandha* (the Preface to the Precepts) up to the *Triṃśan-dharmāḥ* (the Thirty [Naiḥsargika-pāyantikās]), this is the first way of upholding the Vinaya;
if one recites from the *Śīlaskandha* up to the *Navati-prakaraṇāni* (the Ninety Matters), this is the second way of upholding the Vinaya;
if one recites the Vinaya of the Prātimokṣa in its entirety, this is the third way of upholding the Vinaya.
If one extensively recites both divisions of the Vinaya, this is the fourth way of upholding the Vinaya;
if one extensively recites the Vinaya alone, this is the fifth way of upholding the Vinaya.
Among these, during spring and winter, one must rely upon [the guidance of] those who uphold the four types of Vinaya; if one violates this, it is a *duṣkṛta* offense.
"One should rely on the fifth [rule] for the summer retreat; if one violates it, it is a *pāyattika* offense.
The Buddha said, "A person who upholds the Vinaya obtains five merits:"
First, the category of ethical discipline is firm;
second, one is skillfully victorious over all enemies;
third, one is fearless in making decisive judgments within the assembly.
"Fourth, to resolve doubts and regrets;
fifth, to skillfully uphold the Vinaya so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time.
The Buddha said:
“There are four kinds of adjudicators:

one who is of little learning and lacks a sense of shame, and one who is of great learning yet lacks a sense of shame. When such persons speak and adjudicate matters within the Saṃgha, the Saṃgha should reprimand them with various forms of stern admonition so that those lacking a sense of shame shall not do so again.”

Whether one who possesses a sense of shame is learned or whether one who possesses a sense of shame is of little learning, when they speak or adjudicate matters within the assembly, the Saṃgha should provide various forms of assistance and instruction; if they follow what has been said, the Saṃgha should praise them, saying, "Excellent!"
The Buddha said:
"There are five ways in which the True Dharma is swiftly extinguished:
there are bhikṣus who do not carefully receive and recite the Vinaya; they easily forget the words and phrases, yet they teach others with texts that are incomplete and meanings that are deficient."

Second, there are those who are eminent elders among the Saṃgha, yet they frequently fail to maintain the precepts and cultivate only what is unwholesome; others subsequently emulate them and abandon their practice of the precepts.

Third, there are bhikṣus who uphold the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā, yet they do not instruct either the laity or the clergy; consequently, when they pass away, they cause the Dharma to be extinguished.
Fourth, there are bhikṣus who are difficult to instruct and do not accept wholesome words; other virtuous bhikṣus then simply abandon them.
"5. They will revile one another and seek out each other's faults, causing the True Dharma to perish quickly.
The Buddha said:

"If an elder neither trains in the precepts nor praises the precepts, and if there are other bhikṣus who delight in training in the precepts and praising them, yet he fails to encourage, exhort, or praise them at the proper time, I do not praise such an elder."
Why is this? If I were to praise them, it would cause the bhikṣus to draw near to and study their teachings, whereby they would suffer for a long night.
Seeing such faults in these elders, I therefore do not praise them.
If it is a monk of middle or lower seniority, the phrasing is to be applied in the same manner as above.
Next, there are monks of superior, middling, and inferior seniority who are able to praise the precepts; the Buddha praised such a monk of superior seniority in this way.

The phrase "contrary to the above" refers to this. The Buddha said: "There are five ways of answering regarding the Vinaya: [1] *pṛcchā* (questioning); [2] *anupṛcchā* (re-questioning); [3] *vyākaraṇa* (direct answer); [4] *sthāpanīya* (to be set aside); and [5] *paripṛcchā* (answering by asking)."
I. Response concerning the introduction;
II. Response concerning the formal enactment;
III. Response concerning the re-enactment.
"Fourth is the answer according to the sūtras;
fifth is the answer in accordance with the sūtras.
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If one wishes to obtain the benefit of five matters, one should uphold the Vinaya:
first, to establish the Buddha-dharma;
second, to cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time."
Third, not wishing to have doubts or regrets, one asks others for clarification;
fourth, one acts as a refuge for monks and nuns who are terrified by their transgressions;
fifth, one desires to travel and transform beings in all directions without hindrance.
"These are the five benefits for one who faithfully upholds the Vinaya.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"The bhikṣus neglected the study of the Vinaya and instead devoted themselves to reciting and studying the Sūtras and the Abhidharma."
After the World-Honored One had rebuked them in various ways, he praised the Vinaya.
Many elder bhikṣus then went to Upāli to study the Vinaya.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“There are ten kinds of dharmas that, when present in the world, cause the True Dharma to perish quickly: there are bhikṣus who are free from desire but dull-witted;

though they recite the words and meanings, they cannot correctly receive them, nor do they understand them. They are unable to inspire reverence or dignified deportment in those who receive their teachings, and so forth, up to not delighting in the dharma of *āraṇya* (forest dwelling), nor following the instructions of the Dharma. They do not respect their seniors and lack dignified deportment, causing those born later not to study the *vinaya*. This leads to negligence and the loss of all wholesome dharmas. Because they delight in composing literary verses and adorning phrases, and because they take pleasure in worldly dharmas, the True Dharma perishes quickly—this is truly to be feared.”
"Monks, you should know and see it thus.
The *Vibhāṣā* says: "The Buddha said to Ānanda:"
"After my parinirvāṇa, there shall be five dharmas by which the Dharma will abide for a long time:
first, the Vinaya is your Great Teacher;
second, even down to a group of five people who uphold the Vinaya shall remain in the world."
Third, if there are ten persons in the central lands or five persons in the borderlands who receive the precepts according to the Dharma;
fourth, even twenty persons may emerge from transgressions;
fifth, because of the presence of masters of the Vinaya who uphold the discipline, the Buddha-dharma shall remain in the world for five thousand years.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"The Vinaya possesses four meanings not found in other sūtras:
first, it is the level ground of the Buddha-dharma, from which all myriad virtues grow and flourish."
Second, all disciples of the Buddha abide by relying upon the precepts, and all sentient beings exist because of the precepts;
third, they are the initial gateway to Nirvana;
fourth, they are the jeweled ornaments of the Buddha-dharma, capable of adorning the Buddha-dharma.
"Endowed with these four meanings, its merit is superior to that.
The Buddha said:
"There are four kinds of extensive explanations."
If a bhikṣu speaks thus:
"Venerable sirs!
In such-and-such a village or such-and-such a city, I personally heard and received this from the Buddha; this is the Dharma, this is the Vinaya, this is the teaching of the Buddha."
"If you hear what that bhikṣu has said, you should not give rise to suspicion, nor should you rebuke him.
You should first carefully determine the words and phrases, then investigate the Sūtras and the Vinaya, and examine the legal codes."
If, upon listening to what that bhikṣu says, you find it does not correspond with the Sūtras, the Vinaya, or the Dharma and Discipline, and is contrary to the Dharma, you should say to that bhikṣu:
"What you have said was not spoken by the Buddha; or perhaps the Elder has not carefully grasped the Buddha’s words."
Why is this? Upon examining the sūtras, the vinaya, and the legal codes, I find that [this] does not correspond with them; it contradicts the Dharma, Elder!
"There is no further need to recite or practice this, nor should you teach it to other bhikṣus; it should now be abandoned.
If, upon hearing what that bhikṣu has said, one investigates the Sūtras or the Vinaya and finds that it accords with the Dharma and the Vinaya, one should say to him:
"What the Elder has spoken was spoken by the Buddha; he has truly grasped the Buddha's words."
Why is this? I have investigated the Sūtras, the Vinaya, and the legal codes, and they are consistent with one another and do not contradict each other, O Elder!
"You should skillfully maintain and recite it, and teach it to other bhikṣus so that it is not forgotten.
This is the first detailed exposition.
The second phrase was heard from the presence of the Elder of the harmonious Saṃgha.
The third case refers to hearing [the teaching] from before three bhikṣus who know the Dharma, the Vinaya, and uphold the Mātṛkā;
the fourth case refers to hearing it from one bhikṣu who knows the Dharma, the Vinaya, and the Mātṛkā.
The same applies to the acceptance or rejection of words according to whether they are consistent or contradictory with the Dharma.
These are called the four detailed expositions. Therefore, O Bhikṣus!
"You all should follow these words and phrases; do not add to or subtract from them, nor act in violation of the Dharma or the Vinaya. You should train yourselves in this way.
When the Buddha had spoken thus, the bhikṣus heard it and, with joy, faith, and delight, received and upheld it.

From the *Sifen lü shanbu suiji jiemó*, Scroll Lower: The Text for Requesting the *Karmavācanā* for an Aged or Sick Bhikṣu to Possess a Staff and a Net Bag; The Text for Requesting the *Karmavācanā* for an Aged or Sick Bhikṣu to Possess a Staff and a Net Bag. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

I, the bhikṣu [Name], am old and infirm; I am unable to walk without a staff and a carrying net. I now request from the Saṃgha permission to possess a staff and a carrying net. May the Saṃgha, out of compassion, grant me, the bhikṣu [Name], permission to possess a staff and a carrying net.
Thus it was said three times.

The *karmavācanā* for the Sangha’s authorization for an elderly or infirm bhikṣu to possess a staff and a carrying net: "Venerable Sangha, listen! The *karmavācanā* for the Sangha’s authorization for an elderly or infirm bhikṣu to possess a staff and a carrying net: 'Venerable Sangha, listen!'"
The bhikṣu [Name], being old and sickly, is unable to walk without a staff and a carrying net; he now requests the Saṃgha for permission to keep a staff and a carrying net.
If the time is right for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha graciously grant its consent:
that the bhikṣu [Name] shall keep a staff and a carrying net.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
The bhikṣu [Name], being aged and infirm, is unable to walk without a staff and a carrying net; he now requests permission from the Saṃgha to possess a staff and a carrying net."
The Saṃgha now authorizes this bhikṣu to keep a staff and a pouch for it.
Those elders who consent to the motion—"The Saṃgha authorizes bhikṣu so-and-so to keep a staff and a pouch"—should remain silent; those who do not consent should speak.
“The Sangha has already consented, having heard the motion that ‘the bhikṣu so-and-so shall keep a staff and a pouch for it.
Since the Sangha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

The bhikṣu Daoxuan, during the Zhenguan era of the Tang dynasty, traveled among various centers of Vinaya study to extensively seek out diverse methods. He found, however, that people merely recited the texts and placed their trust in the literal words; while the sections were organized into established schools, when it came to discussing the essential points, they had never yet reached the correct principle. Thereupon, he turned his attention to pen and ink and compiled this work according to the fundamental principles of the school.

Although I have not exhausted the origins nor investigated the ends, I hope to provide sufficient resolution for practical application; I wish that this humble offering, like dust and dew before the mountains and seas, may illuminate ten thousand generations, for where my aspirations reach is indeed far-reaching.

The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: Text for the Ordination of the Thirty-nine Night *Karma*. From the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*: Text for the Ordination of the Thirty-nine Night *Karma*. "Venerable Saṃgha, listen!..."

The bhikṣus named so-and-so have received a thirty-nine-night leave of absence for the sake of monastic business and shall depart from the boundary to observe the rains retreat and perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at that location.
If it is the proper time for the Saṃgha, may the Saṃgha grant its consent:

the bhikṣus named so-and-so and so-and-so have received a thirty-nine-night leave of absence for the sake of monastic business and shall depart from the boundary to observe the rains retreat and perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at that location.
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!

Such-and-such bhikṣus have received the thirty-nine-night [permission] and have gone out of the boundary for the sake of monastic business; they shall observe the rains retreat and perform the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at this location."

"Whichever elders approve that 'so-and-so and so-and-so bhikṣus shall receive a thirty-nine-night leave from the monastery for the sake of monastic business, remaining in retreat and performing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at this location,' let them remain silent; whoever does not approve, let them speak."

"The Sangha has already consented, having heard [the proposal]: 'Let the bhikṣus, so-and-so and so-and-so, receive thirty-nine nights' leave from the boundary for the sake of Sangha business, while remaining in residence and performing the *pravāraṇā* ceremony at this location. This is concluded."
"Because the Saṃgha has consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.

Regarding the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* rules on receiving the "remaining night" (*śeṣarātra*): If a bhikṣu receives the seven-night [permission] and returns before it has expired, yet his business remains unfinished, the Buddha said:
"I allow him to receive the remaining night and depart."
“I have received the seven-night rule; with so many nights remaining, I shall receive [the permission] to depart.
This is said once.

The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* concludes the *karmavācanā* text for the twenty-seven matters. Regarding the *karmavācanā* text for the twenty-seven matters in the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*: if it is for the sake of a stūpa matter or a saṃgha matter, one should perform the *anujñā-prārthanā-karman* (the formal act of requesting permission).
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
A certain bhikṣu is observing the rains retreat here at this place.

If the time has come for the Saṃgha, let the Saṃgha permit this bhikṣu, who is observing the rains retreat here, to go beyond the boundary on account of matters concerning the stūpa or matters concerning the Saṃgha, so that he may return to stay here."
"Venerable sirs, listen!
This bhikṣu named [Name] has gone beyond the boundary for the sake of the stūpa or for the sake of the Saṃgha, intending to return to this place for the rains retreat.
Since the Saṃgha consents by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld."
"Thus departing, one must have something to obtain.
Having finished this, he returned at night.
Generally, in the various Vinayas, the methods for receiving the *jīvitādhiṣṭhāna* (authorization to remain beyond the term) also differ from one another.
Later masters who engaged in practical application each adhered to one specific school and did not employ those of other schools; this too constitutes one tradition.
Now, upon examining the Vinaya texts of these various schools, as well as their mutual usage in the past, it is clear that all are permissible.

The reason for this is as follows: if one knows with certainty that a prior matter requires exactly one night, one should employ the method for receiving the "one-night" (*ekarātra*) rite according to the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations); the same applies up to seven nights. If thirty-nine nights are required, one likewise employs the method for receiving the rite through the *Karmavācanā* (Formal Act) of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*.
If seven days, fifteen days, or one month are required, one employs the method for receiving the "days" (*divasa*) according to the text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
If the duration of the prior matter is uncertain, such as how many days it will take to conclude, one employs the method for receiving the "days" according to the text of the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*.

Later, there were those who did not understand this; they would recite the *karmavācanā* text of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* to perform for others the procedure for receiving the *Mahāsāṃghika* precepts, yet fail to recite the "thirty-nine nights" formula. All such cases are contrary to the Dharma and are invalid.
How is this known?
Because the matters recorded within the *karmavācanā* texts differ from one another, we know that [the previous practices] were not valid.

Now, fearing that others might employ them erroneously, I have transcribed the authentic *karmavācanā* texts from various Vinaya schools and presented them to you, worthy sirs, so that you may observe the procedures and apply them according to the specific matter at hand.
"Venerable Saṃgha, listen!
If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha permits,
let so many bhikṣus assemble to establish a small boundary (sīmā)."
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
So many bhikṣus have assembled to establish a minor boundary (sīmā)."
"Whichever elders consent to 'the assembly of so many bhikṣus to establish a small boundary' (sīmābandha) should remain silent; whoever does not consent should speak.
The Saṃgha has already consented to 'the assembly of so many bhikṣus to establish a small boundary'."

If it is a dissolution [of the boundary], simply change the character "jie" (bind) to "jie" (dissolve); all other texts are as previously described for the small boundary, the *pravāraṇā*, and the seated assembly.

If the time has come for the Saṃgha and the Saṃgha is willing to grant its consent:
the seating places for the bhikṣus are already full; let a small boundary (sīmā) be established up to these seating places of the bhikṣus."
The motion is as follows:
"Venerable Sangha, listen!
Within the area defined by the seating places of these bhikṣus, the Sangha shall establish a small boundary (sīmā)."

"Because the Saṃgha has consented by remaining silent, this matter is thus upheld.
